title: NVIDIA has released the weights for MotionBricks on HuggingFace
author: Recoil42
selftext:
[https://huggingface.co/nvidia/MotionBricks](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/MotionBricks)

MotionBricks generates real-time motion for game characters and humanoid robots. Give it a character's recent poses and the poses it should reach next, and it generates the movement in between, at 15,000 FPS with 2 ms latency.  

One model trained on 350K+ motion clips with smart primitives for navigation and object interaction — no retraining.

I suspect that in reality this will save time but will not be an all-powerful animation solution like that AI-delusional people in here are suggesting.

EDIT: Nope, I'm actually incorrect - NVidia is overselling the capabilities of the tool. In the fine print, it is a tweening tool. 

So you set the start and end poses of an animation, and hypothetically it figures out how to get there. 

...I have used these AI tweening tools. Up until now, they have all universally sucked ass. Maybe this is the exception to the rule, but I doubt it.

replies.author: Valentinevandal1986
replies.body: Right now I’m just working on the movement controller. The idea is that it’s both the player and ai controller, but the ai itself will account for balance, velocity, angular momentum and then take into account its body scale and movements and plot a route. Think ultimate tag parkour style movement through an environment that it’s never been trained on. That’s the goal at this point. A smart pathing system using Motionbricks to give it realistic animations that fit. Balance is being calculated like a robot would calculate it, predicting where its body will be and then adjusting. So each swing of a sword for instance should be slightly different based on foot position, speed the character is moving and the physical reach of the character. You could give it a wind up so it’s readable but the exact direction would be position dependent

replies.author: Medium_Chemist_4032
replies.body:
That's exactly, how LLMs work.

Humans have at least an advantage of few advanced neural facilities, that look very similar to formal logic and derivation. LLMs are capable of it, but will never put, on their own, a derived fact back into the base fact storage. They are only capable exactly, what the learning dataset taught them, and it's crystalized in the learning phase. You can approximate, to certain extent extended functionality, that is able to be represented by a combination of prelearned concepts, but if something fundamental is missing, you will never be able to put that ability into the model with prompting alone.

Very simple example: they can't orientate themselves well across mutliple relative frame of references in 3d. They can't do it in CAD, or threejs, or anything that requires a true understanding of that changed frame. They can approximate that, with external tools (like calling to python to verify correctness), but won't be able to use it in a constructive way.

EDIT: Plus, they have quite a few significant limitations, that are routinely taped over during the dataset creation phase. For example, no one yet really \*solved\* the reversal problem: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.12288](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.12288)

Disclaimer: I'm a PhD student of Machine Learning

replies.author: mccoypauley
replies.body:
I don’t think anyone here disputes that LLMs have frozen weights and can’t learn new facts that would end up encoded in their weights. What we dispute is the idea that despite that, they cannot be “creative.”

What is your standard for “creative”? What is an example of something that is creative coming out of human beings vs something that is not creative? I take creative to mean, something novel that is not represented (in its complete form) by prior knowledge. A new poem is creative because it’s a novel arrangement of language (prior knowledge) representing a particular idea. The human used prior knowledge of language and cultural meaning to produce it. A solution to a complicated math problem never before conceived of would be creative because it means a human being drew conclusions from prior knowledge nobody else did before. And so I would argue all “creative” work depends on prior knowledge in this way.

Are the various century-old math problems LLMs have provided solutions for not creative and merely “recombinations” of patterns seen during the training phase? If so, how is this different than human creativity I described above, or any human being doing the same thing? Why does a mathematician solving a math problem like this count as creative but not an LLM? I don’t think the answer is “because LLMs can’t modify their weights.” While superficially it’s true “they are only capable, exactly, \[of\] what the learning dataset taught them” in the sense that any emergent solution depends on prior knowledge, isn’t this true of human beings? We can “modify our weights” because we’re continually receiving input from the outside world, but when we produce something “creative” doesn’t that depend on what we have apprehended at that moment in time?

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body: What kind of game are you making? 99% of games can't use this because the time it takes to calculate the animations on the fly is not insignificant and while one actor is manageable, try a tavern full of NPCs or a city. replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
Yes. It's roughly \~17GB when running as fast as possible (arguably playable in a lot of game types, though the delay IS noticeable despite it claiming '2ms', maybe it just feels a lot longer because it's related to input, but it reminds me of playing starcraft or league with 300 or so ping.)  You CAN run it for significantly less, as low as \~8 (supposedly lower if you want to take larger latency hits) but  you're looking at even more delay. I don't know how long. I didn't bother to test that. The only way I could see the tech being useful is if you could export it (at last for the kinds of games I'm interested in).  Like if someone is looking for the realism this gives, then they're probably also wanting a game that feels alive and has a lot of NPCs moving around, which this precludes due to having to calc ALL of them. I guess you could possibly apply it to just the player character. But eh, if your goal is to actually create exportable animations this is not it. I believe Cascadeur is working on real-time animation like that (UE Live Link) and is cheap as hell. And Nvidia does have another product ARDY which DOES do real-time animation that allows for export as actual animation files. That should probably be the go-to for any game developer.

Motion Bricks could be interesting for someone wanting to make a cinematic trailer for their game, though, within the game world, but not want to make a bunch of custom animations for their characters to do one-time things.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
Depends on your definition of animation system. For real-time animation calculation sure. But you can make perfectly realistic looking animation,, and they do so in games like modern assassin's creeds, where there are 10-20 prebaked animations, all parametric and able to adapt to the scene, that your character can swap between when, say, jumping off a cliff, and they're influenced by what your character was doing before (walking, running, cartwheeling, waving their hands, etc). That's perfectly serviceable for realism. Most of us don't have a limitless supply of animations we use in our day to day. If I'm walking I'm 99% of the time using the same stride.

Most games have no use for something that has to calculate a brand new animation on the fly. This is pretty much for a point and click style adventure game, or possibly a turn-based system could incorporate it. Even if the tech improves, it's going to be a constant tradeoff between whether you want adaptive animation or that same performance to be put towards visual fidelity or actor numbers or whatever, and the latter is going to win 99 times out of 100 in terms of relevance to the game.

Sometimes the old ways just work best. And this is one of those times. Until compute is somehow free, precomputing anything you can is key.

That being said, I love the idea of using some of these new real-time animation systems to \*create\* animations on the fly for baking. Though I do like the control Cascadeur gives which I don't really see here.
